extraction.name: Commonsense QA
extraction.description: A question answering challenge targeting commonsense knowledge. The dataset contains 12,247 multiple-choice questions generated from ConceptNet by crowd workers and includes five candidate answers per question.
extraction.creator: Alon Talmor, Jonathan Herzig, Nicholas Lourie, Jonathan Berant
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created by extracting subgraphs from ConceptNet, then using Amazon Mechanical Turk crowd workers to author multiple-choice commonsense questions, add distractors, and verify question quality. Web search snippets were also collected for each question-answer pair by querying Google search.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web API, Experiments
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: ConceptNet triplets/subgraphs were used as the source knowledge base; Google search result snippets were retrieved as textual context.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Triplets were filtered to remove general or already well-explored relations, concepts with more than four words or non-English concepts, and triplets with low edit distance between concepts. Triplets were grouped into question sets of one source concept and three target concepts. For each question, two additional distractors were added, one sampled from ConceptNet and one manually authored. Questions were then verified by separate workers, and only questions verified by at least one correct worker were kept.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: ConceptNet triplets were filtered by relation type, concept length/language, and edit distance. Questions failing verification were removed; 15% of formulated questions were filtered out. For the web-context version, the first 100 Google snippets for each of five answer candidates were collected, yielding 500 snippets per question.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk authored three questions per question set, one per target concept, ensuring the correct answer was one of the target concepts and the other two were not. Workers added two more distractors per question. A disjoint group of workers then verified each question by choosing the right answer or marking it unanswerable. Additionally, 100 development examples were manually annotated for commonsense skill categories.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Each question was verified by 2 workers, and only questions verified by at least one worker who answered correctly were retained. For the commonsense skill analysis, examples could receive multiple skill labels, with an average of 1.75 skills per question.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 2 verifiers per question; skill analysis examples could have multiple labels, average 1.75 skills per question.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk; 122 formulators contributed to question generation, and a separate group of workers performed verification. No further demographics were reported.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google search was used to retrieve web snippets; no other automated annotation tools were reported.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to advance commonsense question answering and improve natural language understanding systems by testing commonsense knowledge beyond surface cues.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes reporting bias in web text and discusses annotation artifacts and distributional biases as concerns in natural language datasets. It also observes that some questions may probe relations other than the intended ConceptNet relation.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to commonsense multiple-choice questions derived from ConceptNet and may not cover all commonsense phenomena. Models still perform far below humans, and web snippets do not provide much useful information. The dataset is not intended for questions requiring specialized scientific knowledge.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development, testing, and evaluation of commonsense question answering models; also used for baseline comparison and analysis. The paper uses an 80/10/10 train/development/test split and evaluates both random and question-concept splits.
